item.title: ‘Is Ambani real boss,’ asks Elon Musk after accusing ‘oligarchs’ of stalling Starlink India launch
item.description: ‘Welcome to India, Elon,’ Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said in response. ‘Wait till you discover the other guy.’
item.content:encoded:
Trillionaire Elon Musk on Thursday asked if “Ambani is the real boss” of India amid an online debate about his Starlink satellite internet network not having received clearance to operate in the country.

“Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?” he asked.

Musk did not specify which member of the Ambani family he was referring to. Scroll has requested comment from Reliance Industries Limited. This report will be updated if we receive a comment.

In a response to Musk’s remark, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said: “Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy.”

Musk was responding to a comment by another social media user who alleged that the Indian government was “more interested in protecting the interests of crony capitalists than of citizens”.

The businessman’s remark came a day after he accused “certain oligarchs” in India of blocking the launch of Starlink, saying that they are trying to protect their “monopolistic chokehold” over the industry.

Starlink provides internet access through a constellation of satellites placed in low-earth orbit by Musk’s spacecraft manufacturing company SpaceX.

item.title: Delhi: Five killed in Seemapuri building collapse
item.description: The bodies were recovered a day after the incident took place on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Five persons were killed after a four-storey building collapsed in northeast Delhi’s Seemapuri on Wednesday, PTI reported.

Three bodies of a pregnant woman, a 12-year-old girl and a child aged around one-and-a-half years were recovered from the site on Thursday.

Later in the day, two more were recovered, PTI quoted an unidentified government official as saying.

The building collapsed at about 3.30 pm on Wednesday, burying portions of two to three adjoining houses under the debris.

Residents said that the building had developed cracks after tremors felt in the national capital because of an earthquake in Uttarakhand on Tuesday. Officials said that the exact cause of the collapse will be investigated.

Eight persons injured in the collapse have been taken to hospital for treatment. Rescue teams were clearing the site.

The incident came a month after a five-storey building in southwest Delhi’s Satya Niketan collapsed on September 6, leaving seven persons dead and 12 injured.

That building was reportedly 40 to 50 years old, and repair work was underway in the basement when it collapsed.

The Delhi High Court had said that “callous and criminal conduct” had led to the incident.

item.title: Onions, sugar, rice: Why India’s food staples have gotten costly
item.description: Poor rainfall, speculation on sugarcane harvesting were among the main reasons.
item.content:encoded:
In September, a kilogram of onion cost 93% more than last year, while sugar prices were up 28% and rice was up about 8%, on average, according to ISignal’s Food Price Watch dashboard, which uses Department of Consumer Affairs data. This is in a year with the fourth lowest rainfall since the turn of the century, as the country approaches the withdrawal of the monsoon with a 13% deficit.

Sustained low prices in past years pushed farmers away from onion, experts say, while the government lists factors such as increased demand and speculation for the increase in sugar prices.

“Extreme climate events are raising agricultural risk, disrupting the global food system, increasing the chance of multiple breadbasket failure and pushing up food prices around the world,” a September 2026 analysis by Zero Carbon Analytics noted, adding that “historically unprecedented heat, drought, rain and cold are causing food price spikes across all continents”.

It also noted that perishable foods such as fruits and vegetables can face larger price swings because of their limited shelf life and more vulnerable supply chains.

ISignal reached out to the Department of Consumer Affairs for comment. We will update this report when we receive a response.

item.title: Andhra Pradesh declares drought in 21 districts as rainfall deficit stands at 53%
item.description: ‘An average rainfall of 197.6 mm has been received against the normal rainfall of 424.3 mm from June 1 to August 31,’ read the government order.
item.content:encoded:
The Andhra Pradesh government has declared a drought in 21 of its 28 districts as the rainfall deficit from June to August in the state stood at 53%, reported The Hindu on Thursday.

The deficit in rainfall was due to the effects of El Niño, which is a phenomenon that involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to reduced monsoon rainfall in India.

“An average rainfall of 197.6 mm has been received against the normal rainfall of 424.3 mm from June 1 to August 31,” The Indian Express quoted the government order as saying.

The government declared the drought for the Kharif season on October 1, reported The Hindu. Such declarations are typically made at the end of October.

The Kharif season in India is between June and October.

The 21 affected districts are Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli, Kakinada, East Godavari, Eluru, Krishna, NTR district, Guntur, Bapatla, Palnadu, Prakasam, Markapuram, Kurnool, Nandyal, Ananthapuramu, Sri Satya Sai, YSR Kadapa, Annamayya and Chittoor.

In September, the Maharashtra government declared drought conditions in 74% of the state’s subdistricts amid a deficit in rainfall during the southwest monsoon season.

item.title: Is 2026 the beginning of the end of the Modi era?
item.description: When protests begin attracting large numbers of people who are willing to risk police beatings, it is usually a sign of anti-incumbency setting in.
item.content:encoded:
In 2011, Delhi became the epicentre of protests that three years later, culminated in the toppling of the Manmohan Singh government.

Fifteen years later, the national capital is once again aflame with protests. Will they similarly build up momentum for political change in 2029?

There are strong parallels between 2011 and 2026.

In 2011, after protests in Jantar Mantar in April, Ramlila Maidan saw two rounds of mass demonstrations – the first in June, the second in August.

This year, barely two months after young people took over Jantar Mantar in June, a second wave is building up, with the police this week blocking even Opposition leaders from reaching the protest square.

In 2011, it was about “corruption”. In 2026, it is about “rigging” – of exam papers, of the election system. This year’s summer protests at Jantar Mantar ended with the resignation of the education minister. Now, protestors are demanding that the chief election commissioner step down for a botched-up revision of electoral rolls that has led to mass voter disenfranchisement.

item.title: Activist Umar Khalid wins international human rights defender award
item.description: His incarceration is evidence of India’s ‘expanding use of anti-terror laws against dissent’, said Ireland-based organisation Front Line Defenders.
item.content:encoded:
Activist Umar Khalid, who has been in prison for more than six years in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case, won the 2026 Award for Human Rights Defenders at Risk on Thursday.

The award is given out by the Ireland-based human rights organisation Front Line Defenders. It was presented at a ceremony in Dublin, which Khalid could not attend.

He was arrested on September 13, 2020, and has remained in jail since then without trial.

The other recipients of this year’s award are Ahmadreza Haeri, an anti-death penalty campaigner from Iran, Laurinda Manuel Gouveia, a feminist pro-participatory democracy defender from Angola, Adda Vyctoria Caetano, a Black trans woman leader from Brazil, and Ljiljana Nešić, a feminist peacebuilder from Serbia.

The police had arrested Khalid in connection with the communal violence that broke out in North East Delhi in February 2020 between supporters of the contentious Citizenship Amendment Act and those opposing it. The violence had left 53 dead and hundreds injured. Most of those killed were Muslims.

item.title: Canadian author, poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson wins the 2026 Nobel Prize for Literature
item.description: She won ‘for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature’.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature was on Thursday awarded to Canadian poet, essayist, translator, classicist, and professor Anne Carson “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”. She is 76, and is the second writer from Canada to win the award (after Alice Munro in 2013).

The prestigious award, bestowed by 18 judges who make up the Swedish Academy, honours a writer’s entire body of work and is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million (about Rs 11.6 crore).

The Nobel Prize website said: “Anne Carson has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities. Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.”

Carson’s oeuvre across forms and genres comprises more than 30 works. Among her notable works are Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse (1998), Norma Jean Baker of Troy: a version of Euripides’ Helen (2019) and translations of Sophocles’s Electra, and of Euripides’s Grief Lessons: Four Plays.

item.title: Stock market slides to 32-month low, investors lose Rs 10 lakh crore
item.description: Foreign funds have sold securities worth $4.8 billion in nine days, taking the net outflows this year to a record $30.4 billion.
item.content:encoded:
The stock market on Thursday fell by 1.4% to a 32-month low amid tighter monetary conditions, increasing global oil prices and continued outflow of foreign funds.

The benchmark Sensex index fell by more than 1,040 points to end just below 71,600. The index was at 75,000 during this time last month. The Nifty 50 fell by 371 points to 22,200, an 18-month low.

Investors lost more than Rs 10 lakh crore during the day.

The India VIX index, which measures volatility in the market, spiked 10%.

Foreign investors have sold securities worth $4.8 billion in nine days, taking the net outflows this year to a record $30.4 billion, Reuters reported.

The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday increased the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5%. This was the first hike in the lending rate in nearly four years.

After the repo rate was revised, the market had fallen by more than half a percent on Wednesday.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks.

Central banks usually increase key lending rates to control inflation. Higher key lending rates translate to higher interest on loans disbursed by commercial banks. This, in turn, keeps a check on discretionary spending by consumers which is expected to help curb price rise due to high inflation.

item.title: US proposes $70,000 fee for foreign students seeking temporary work
item.description: More than 1.4 lakh Indians were participating in the optional practical training programme in the academic year 2024-’25.
item.content:encoded:
The United States has proposed a fee of $70,000, or approximately Rs 67 lakh, for foreign students seeking to participate in the optional practical training programme.

The programme allows foreign students to work in the US for one to two years in fields related to their education after completing their courses.

Under the proposed rule, institutes certified under the Student and Exchange Visitor Program would be required to pay the fee before recommending foreign students for the programme, and before they apply for employment authorisation with US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

More than 3.6 lakh Indian students were studying in the US during the academic year 2024-’25, according to data from the Institute of International Education. Over 1.4 lakh of them were participating in the optional practical training programme during the period.

The Department of Homeland Security said on Wednesday that the move was aimed at reducing the “flow of cheap labour” into the US and “make it easier for American citizens to compete in the job market”.

It also proposed introducing a fee of $30,000, or Rs 29 lakh, for any subsequent participation in the programme.

item.title: Tribute: Nana Patekar was a force of nature
item.description: His intensity was uncomfortable to watch at times. Even when he was quiet, there was the feeling that something inside him was moving.
item.content:encoded:
The world knew him as Nana Patekar. But I knew him as Vishwanath Patekar.

My connection with the actor came through GD Tari and his wife Kamala, whom Nana lovingly called Aai and Baba, or mother and father. I lived next door to the Taris in Kalyan in the 1980s. Before they moved to Kalyan, the Taris resided in Sion, where they first met Patekar.

Patekar had had a troubled childhood. The Tari couple gave Patekar something that mattered more than money or opportunity: a sense of belonging. When he enrolled in the JJ School of Art, they supported him throughout the course, alongside their own sons. He never forgot it.

In 1986, after Patekar gained popularity with the film Ankush, he dropped into Birla College in Kalyan. The crowds were huge, so when GD Tari got there, he had no way to get in.

My sister and I were accompanying Tari. When Patekar returned to his car, Tari tapped on the window. Patekar leapt out of the car and hugged Tari, repeatedly saying, baba, tumhi aalat. Father, you are finally here.

The Delhi Election Commission on Wednesday said that it will organise special camps to ensure that voters whose homes have been demolished recently are not excluded from the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

This came amid concerns over deletions of names from the electoral rolls during the voter list revision exercise. The Election Commission has directed the 20 states and Union territories where the exercise has concluded to conduct a special drive to enroll voters who were “left out” of the electoral rolls, The Indian Express reported.

In Delhi, 47.7 lakh voters were removed from the draft electoral rolls prepared as part of the SIR. The draft list has 97.5 lakh voters. The names not included in the draft roll account for 33% of the Union Territory’s electorate.

Those removed from the voter list were marked as either permanently shifted, deceased, absent, duplicate entries or placed under the “other” category. It was unclear what the “other” category referred to.

Verification of such cases is to be completed by October 29, while the final electoral rolls are slated to be published on November 4.

item.description: Flaws in the Election Commission’s online platform set were flagged to the poll panel in July by a researcher, the ‘Hindustan Times’ reported on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
The Congress on Thursday alleged that the Election Commission’s online portal for voter registration and related services was designed to “centralise all deletions and additions from the Bharatiya Janata Party headquarters”.

The allegation came after the Hindustan Times reported that a security researcher had in July flagged vulnerabilities in the poll panel’s voter-services website and ECINET application to the Election Commission and the country’s cyber-security agency, CERT-In.

He had warned that the flaws could expose election officials’ contact details and allow attackers to access or forge data on the application.

Nisarga Adhikary emailed CERT-In on July 8, copying the Election Commission’s complaints address. Nearly three months later, on Monday, Hindustan Times sent questions to both agencies about his findings and did not receive a response.

However, on the next day, CERT-In replied to Adhikary, saying one vulnerability had been fixed and work on the others was “under progress”. It was not clear when the reported fix had been made.

A critical vulnerability indentified by the researcher involved a server that could return the names and mobile numbers of election officials without requiring a login or CAPTCHA security test. item.title: Gauhati HC rejects woman’s citizenship plea, says ‘sympathy cannot be misapplied’
item.description: Interest of the country must be given ‘paramount consideration’, it held, while upholding a 2017 order declaring Hasena Bhanu a foreigner.
item.content:encoded:
The Gauhati High Court on Monday rejected a woman’s plea challenging a 2017 tribunal order that declared her a foreigner, saying “sympathy cannot be misapplied” in cases involving undocumented migrants and foreigners, The Indian Express reported.

The interest of the country must be given “paramount consideration”, the bench said. It held that Mustt Hasena Bhanu had failed to provide sufficient documentary evidence to establish her Indian citizenship and her claimed family links, the newspaper reported.

The court was hearing Bhanu’s challenge to a May 19, 2017, order of a foreigners’ tribunal, which had declared her a foreigner who entered India after March 25, 1971.

The tribunal had found that she failed to establish her links to the people she identified as her father and grandfather.

The foreigners tribunals in Assam are quasi-judicial bodies that adjudicate on matters of citizenship based on lineage and a 1971 cut-off date. They rely primarily on documents submitted by persons to establish their family’s residency in Assam or India before 1971.

Those declared foreigners by the tribunals have the option to appeal the decision before the High Court or the Supreme Court.

item.title: Actor Nana Patekar dies at 75
item.description: He was found unconscious in his Goa home early in the morning.
item.content:encoded:
Veteran actor Nana Patekar died at the age of 75 after suffering a cardiac arrest at his home in Goa on Thursday, PTI reported.

Patekar was found unconscious at his apartment early in the morning and was taken to hospital, the news agency quoted the doctor at the medical facility as saying.

Despite being administered cardiopulmonary resuscitation for 45 minutes, Patekar could not be revived and was declared dead at 5.20 am.

A medico-legal case has been registered and a postmortem will be conducted.

According to information provided by a friend of Patekar to doctors, the actor had messaged him around 3.30 am saying he was not feeling well. The friend saw the message around 4 am and went to Patekar’s apartment, where he was living with a caretaker, PTI reported.

Patekar’s body has been sent to Goa Medical College and Hospital in Bambolim for a postmortem to ascertain the exact cause of death.

Patekar was known for his roles in several Hindi and Marathi films. His notable Hindi films include Parinda, Prahaar: The Final Attack, Tirangaa, Krantiveer and Khamoshi: The Musical.

He was a recipient of three National Film Awards, several Filmfare Awards and the Maharashtra State Film Award. He was also awarded the Padma Shri, the country’s fourth-highest civilian honour, in 2013.

item.title: Punjab’s prisons are awash with de-addiction pills. But is that good news?
item.description: The High Court and an assembly panel have flagged the surge in supply to jails. Some experts say this may be a sign of growing addiction.
item.content:encoded:
In 2017, the Punjab government introduced a new therapy for victims of drug abuse.

It involved putting users of opioids like heroin – colloquially called chitta – on a combination of less potent opioids to wean them off their addiction.

The substitute – buprenorphine and naloxone pills – was meant to be taken orally and under medical supervision. According to a psychiatrist who works in one of Punjab’s central jails, the therapy drastically reduced the vulnerability of an addict.

“Firstly, there is no intravenous use because of which an addict is likely to get infected with HIV, hepatitis or other diseases,” he said. “There is almost zero chance of drug overdose death.”

The therapy was rolled out across more than 529 clinics over the years and met with limited success. In November 2023, the Punjab government informed the Assembly that around 80-90% of patients who complete this treatment at the state’s Outpatient Opioid Assisted Treatment clinics relapse into addiction.

Strikingly, in the last four years, the supply of buprenorphine pills to Punjab’s prisons has surged and the number of inmates registered with deaddiction clinics has doubled, the Punjab government’s figures show.

item.title: Maritime history: How merchants transcended caste and faith identity to rule over sea trade
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Indians in the Ocean: Cultures of Trade and Travel ca 1000-1500 CE’, by Mahmood Kooria.
item.content:encoded:
Major maritime merchant communities from the subcontinent transcended religious, regional and caste identities. In the existing literature, they are often identified along these lines, yet such classifications do not fully capture the fluid and interconnected nature of their networks, as in the case of Banias, which included Buddhists and Jains earlier, but also Hindus and even Muslims later. The same goes with Lohanas as well as Klings and Chulias, all who crossed the borders of religions as much as of the regions. It would be impossible to enlist and analyse all mercantile groups from the subcontinent here, but below I provide snapshots of a few major transoceanic communities active between the 11th and 16th centuries.

Until the end of the first millennium in the subcontinent, Buddhist and Jain traders played a major role in the oceanic world, often mirroring their influence in overland commerce. The boundaries between these groups in the maritime mercantile contexts were blurry, but we do see occasional references for them competing for economic and political influence.

For instance, in the Maitraka kingdom of Vallabhi in Gujarat, Jain and Buddhist merchants were in fiercest competition. The major competitors of the Jain traders of Vallabhi were the Buddhist merchants from Bharuch...

item.title: What questions and debates in Parliament say about India’s climate change priorities
item.description: There was a focus on energy and forests but financial and institutional dimensions of climate action were less examined.
item.content:encoded:
India, like other countries, is grappling with the effects of El Niño, which has exacerbated global warming, causing a major rainfall deficit in the country this year. Over the past decade, India has seen climate change take a deadly toll in the form of extreme weather and disasters such as landslides and glacial collapse.

How did these concerns resonate in the Indian Parliament?

In the last 10 years, Parliament maintained a steady focus on climate change, but its attention has centered largely on setting ambitious goals and announcing national targets.

My analysis of the environmental-related questions discussed in Parliament over the last 10 years found that the focus was on sectors such as energy and forests. The financial and institutional dimensions of climate action received considerably less attention.

The report titled “Climate on the Floor: India’s Parliamentary Discourse on Environment since the Paris Agreement” was released by the Centre for Financial Accountability on October 2. It analysed the questions raised in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha between December 2015 and December 2025, along with parliamentary debates. India was among the 200 countries that adopted the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement on reducing carbon emissions.

item.title: Three years since October 7, Gaza has faded from headlines. All eyes are now on Israel’s elections
item.description: If a less extreme government takes office after the polls on October 27, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank hold?
item.content:encoded:
This week marks three years since Hamas’ massacre of October 7, 2023, in which some 1,200 people, most of them Israeli civilians, were killed and 251 taken hostage.

What followed were two years of devastating war waged by the Israel Defense Forces in Gaza, which a United Nations commission of inquiry, leading genocide scholars and major human rights organisations have concluded amounted to genocide. Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.

A year ago this week, a US-imposed ceasefire was finally forced on both sides – though mainly on paper. While major IDF assaults have ceased, Israeli attacks in Gaza have continued, in addition to unbridled Jewish settler violence in the West Bank.

Despite this, global attention on Gaza has waned. As the US-Israeli war with Iran began dominating the headlines, earlier pledges by many states to help drive the peace process forward have proved once again wanting, even hollow.

Now, Israel is preparing for a highly polarised parliamentary election on October 27, which could be consequential for the entire region. If a less extreme government takes office, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank – and the pressure it has generated – hold?

item.title: Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win chemistry Nobel for research into mirror-image molecules
item.description: Discoveries by them have been ‘decisive’ for developing pharmaceuticals, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded on Wednesday to two chemists for their research into the mirror images of molecules, which is decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.

Henri Kagan, 95, is a professor at the Université Paris-Sud in France. He is a French citizen. Kenso Soai, a 76-year-old Japanese citizen, is a professor at the Tokyo University of Science.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said that they were being honoured for the discovery of “non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.

Some molecules, such as amino acids, exist as two variants that are each other’s mirror image. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror images.

“How chemical asymmetry such as this could have emerged was long a mystery to chemists,” the academy said, adding that Kagan and Soai discovered “a solution to this puzzle”.

Their discoveries have been “decisive for chemists who design reactions” for manufacturing pharmaceuticals, it added.

The two chemists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish kronor, or Rs 11.5 crore.

The Nobel Prize in literature will be announced on Thursday and for peace on Friday. The prize in economics will be announced on October 12.

item.title: RBI raises repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% amid rising inflation
item.description: This was the first hike in the lending rate in four years.
item.content:encoded:
The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday increased the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5%.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks. The Monetary Policy Committee reviews the rate every two months.

This was the first hike in the lending rate in nearly four years. The last hike was in February 2023, when the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 6.5%.

Central banks usually increase key lending rates to control inflation. Higher key lending rates translate to higher interest on loans disbursed by commercial banks. This, in turn, keeps a check on discretionary spending by consumers which is expected to help curb price rise due to high inflation.

The committee had cut the repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.5% to 5.25% in December and kept it unchanged in February, April, June and August.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Basis points are used to describe changes in interest rates and other financial instruments.

The committee also changed its monetary policy stance to “calibrated tightening” from “neutral”. The shift signals that the central bank is now more focused on containing inflation.

The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 signalled the end of the Soviet Union. This, in its wake, unfroze conflicts across the globe that were sustained by the West in the Cold War. I remember how Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and other Commonwealth leaders failed to persuade Britain’s Margaret Thatcher at a 1986 summit in London to stiffen sanctions against apartheid. Thatcher’s reaction was rigid because the Soviet paranoia still plagued the West. That is why she advanced a lame excuse for not weakening the White apartheid regime.

“More sanctions would hurt Black workers,” she argued.

Likewise, Italy’s Christian Democrats were kept in power despite unspeakable corruption, much of which came to light only after the Soviet threat had ended in 1991. item.description: In Rejinagar, Scroll found that the police were intimidating Muslim voters, detaining Opposition workers and stifling journalists.
item.content:encoded:
An Assembly bye-poll in West Bengal on Tuesday saw the administration making widespread attempts at rigging it in favour of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, Opposition workers alleged.

In Rejinagar, where the bye-election was held, Scroll found that the police were turning away Muslim voters from some polling stations, intimidating Opposition workers and stifling independent journalists.

When asked about this, Harshal Pancholi, an Indian Administrative Service officer serving as the Election Commission’s general observer in Rejinagar, asserted that the bye-poll was “free and fair”. He said that after political parties alleged that some booths had been captured, he had examined “video evidence” and was satisfied with the manner in which voting was conducted.

item.title: Bangladesh measles outbreak claims 900 lives – and serves as warning for why vaccination matters
item.description: Even a small dip in vaccination rates can leave pockets of unprotected children.
item.content:encoded:
Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.

Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. It can spread rapidly when vaccination rates fall, and the Bangladesh outbreak shows how quickly years of gaps in protection can turn into a serious public health crisis.

The country had hoped to eliminate measles and rubella by 2020. Instead, the pandemic disrupted routine childhood vaccinations, leaving pockets of children vulnerable to the virus. Now other countries where vaccination rates have fallen face a similar risk.

Vaccine hesitancy is probably part of the story here too. During the Covid pandemic, almost half of Bangladesh’s population were wary of getting vaccinated. That same wariness may well have carried over to the measles-rubella jab, with many parents simply refusing to let their children be vaccinated.

Measles has its own set of drivers, too. Poverty, education levels, and how often mothers attend antenatal check-ups all shape whether children in a community end up vaccinated. Add it all up, and childhood vaccination coverage has been sliding for years – down to just 87%.

item.title: Francis Halzen awarded physics Nobel for discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin
item.description: His ‘vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental’ for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Physics was on Tuesday awarded to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin and his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

Halzen, 82, is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States.

“His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

The observatory is near the South Pole in Antarctica. Using the observatory, researchers “can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe”, the academy added.

Halzen first presented his vision for capturing neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the glacial ice.

He will receive a prize amount of 12 million Swedish krona, or Rs 11.5 crore.

On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was jointly awarded to three scientists – Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth – for their research on brain activity.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry will be announced on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and for peace on Friday. The prize in economics will be announced on October 12.

item.title: The world order is ‘complicated’. Can Indian foreign policy navigate ‘situationships’?
item.description: New Delhi’s global posturing has always coexisted with a pragmatic practice closer to home.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s much-discussed special address at Davos in January called for a world of “values-based realism.” First proposed by Finland’s President, Alexander Stubb, values-based realism describes not a strategy, but an “instrument – temporary, adaptive, and situational…that espouses values while engaging respectfully with those who do not share them.”

Put more colloquially, this macro-geopolitical landscape operates exactly like a Gen Z “situationship” – relationships that are not beholden to labels, exclusivity, and can be non-committal.

India, with its cautious diplomatic language and history of moral rhetoric on the global stage, may not seem like a player suited to this new world of “situationships.” Yet New Delhi’s record navigating problematic regimes in its own neighborhoods suggests that India may actually enter this new order with more experience than most.

item.title: How El Niño is causing droughts in parts of the world and floods elsewhere
item.description: It is a result of climactic conditions being shaped by the warming Pacific Ocean and the air above it.
item.content:encoded:
The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year’s El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

El Niño, the warm phase of a natural fluctuation in the Earth’s climate system, can reshape weather thousands of miles away, bringing drought to some regions while increasing the risk of heavy rain and flooding in others. To understand why, you need to follow what happens to the Pacific’s warm water – and the air above it.

Usually, winds over the tropical Pacific blow from east to west, pushing warm surface water towards the western Pacific, where it piles up around Indonesia and nearby regions. These are the trade winds. As warm water moves westward, colder water from deeper in the ocean rises to replace it in the east – a process called upwelling. This is why the western Pacific is usually much warmer than the eastern Pacific.

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was on Monday jointly awarded to three scientists for their work on light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

Peter Hegemann from Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg in Germany discovered a protein, named channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga.

Karl Deisseroth from The Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University in the United States developed a way to turn the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells.

Their research has fundamentally changed the way science understands the human brain, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet said in a statement. The three scientists have “laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience”, it added.

Their research has led to the discovery of a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the brain, the Nobel Assembly said.

Researchers are using the method to try and restore eyesight in people.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, the chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.

item.title: ‘If you are good, people will automatically contact you,’ says mridangam player TS Nandakumar
item.description: In August, the US-based percussionist received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in the Overseas category.
item.content:encoded:
For 68-year-old TS Nandakumar, the journey from Mumbai to America has been shaped by music, but also by the people he encountered along the way.

He arrived in Mumbai from Keralam in the late 1970s as a young mridangam player and gradually became part of a remarkable musical ecosystem, accompanying some of the most respected names of the era.

MD Ramanathan, M Balamuralikrishna and Bhimsen Joshi were among the legendary musicians with whom he shared the stage. Mumbai gave him a performing career, students and friendships that remain deeply etched in his memory. That’s why he was given the moniker “Bombay” Nandakumar.

When Nandakumar eventually moved to the US in 2008, it meant leaving behind a musical world in which he had already established himself. The early years were not easy. He spent nine years without his family, travelling long distances to teach and perform. It was music that sustained him through that period, he said.

Today, with students across countries, 50 who have done arangetrams [debut dance performances] and books documenting his knowledge, Nandakumar sees the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in the Overseas category he received in August as both recognition and responsibility.

item.title: Why an anonymous X post about anti-caste readings got the PMO’s attention
item.description: Most of the works cited in the X post contain arguments critical of the caste system and, in some instances, Hindutva.

Periyar EV Ramasamy, one of the leading figures of the Dravidian movement, argued that “To insist that chastity is only for women and should not be insisted upon for men, is a philosophy based on biased individual ownership.” As part of the argument, published in his Collected Works, he noted further that “If our literatures have all been written for the sake of justice and disciplined conduct, then, should not all the conditions imposed on women be applied to men too.”

To many academics, these arguments remain relevant and vital even today, and students stand to gain significantly from reading and engaging with them. To their shock, however, the book was among the publications that the Prime Minister’s Office took note of after an anonymous X user included it in a list of material that the user termed “poison”.

item.title: Can a messy person change or are some people just naturally tidier?
item.description: Personality isn’t destiny and changing patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.
item.content:encoded:
Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the wardrobe, and their kitchen bench remains mysteriously visible.

Others can clean the house on Sunday and wonder by Wednesday how everything became messy again.

It’s tempting to explain this as personality: “I’m just a messy person.” And there is some truth to that. But personality isn’t destiny. Our surroundings and the small things we repeatedly do within them matter too.

In fact, changing those patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.

Are some people just naturally tidier?

Psychologists describe personality in terms of relatively enduring patterns in how people tend to think, feel and behave.

One of the “Big Five” personality traits is conscientiousness. It includes tendencies towards being industrious, self-controlled and orderly. So, someone higher in conscientiousness – particularly its orderliness aspects – may find keeping things organised easier.

But “relatively enduring” doesn’t mean personality is fixed.

Large studies following people over time show personality is both stable and changeable. For example, people tend to become more conscientious during different stages of adulthood, such as when they have children or new responsibilities.

So, saying “I’m a messy person” may describe a tendency. It doesn’t condemn you to a lifetime of losing your keys.

item.title: How a love of gossip could make you a better reader

Much of the discussion of the book revolves around the similarities between Portman’s real life rather than how Cusk explores her chosen themes. In a recent article for The Guardian, journalist Elle Hunt provides a handy list of must-know information for those wishing to read the novel but may be unsure of all the details. The biogossip argument is certainly plausible. For instance, references to Léon: The Professional (1994) and Black Swan (2010) are easy enough to pick up if you are aware of Portman’s filmography. At the conclusion, Hunt asks whether more gossip in literature could solve the crisis of people reading less than ever.

item.title: These websites give you the thrill of online shopping without buying anything
item.description: A new trend emerging in South Korea allows users to browse products, place and order and even track its ‘delivery’.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

This week, I placed orders for a $44,860 Patek Philippe hand-engraved watch, a $12,500 Hermès handbag, a $9,800 Tiffany diamond ring, and a $7,350 Cartier Love bracelet in yellow gold.

I don’t need any of them. I certainly can’t afford them. Thankfully, they’ll never arrive.

Instead of Amazon, I spent the past week browsing a new breed of websites known as “dopamine sites,” a trend that emerged in South Korea. These websites – like Dopamine Shop and FoodNeverComes – recreate the entire ritual of online shopping: You search for products, compare reviews, add items to your cart, enter a shipping address, place an order, and even track your delivery.

Then … nothing happens. No money changes hands. No package arrives.

It’s tempting to dismiss them as another quirky internet trend. But after spending a week placing imaginary orders, I found myself wondering if online shopping has stopped being solely about buying things.

item.title: Sunday book pick: Simone de Beauvoir’s ‘A Very Easy Death’ is a moving memoir about her dying mother
item.description: The memoir was originally published in French in 1964 as ‘Une Morte Très Douce.’ It was translated by Patrick O’Brian in 1965.

“Her heart was in excellent condition and her blood pressure was that of a young woman: I had never been afraid of a sudden mishap for her.”

Simone de Beauvoir’s A Very Easy Death, a memoir about her dying mother, is the perfect read if you’re looking to fill a Mother Mary Comes to Me-sized hole in your heart.

An age to die

Beauvoir begins the story of her mother Françoise’s death with the news of her breaking the neck of her femur after a fall in the bathroom. Her neighbours call her daughters, Simone and Poupette, who immediately rush to the scene. Françoise is addressed as maman by her daughters and at 77, Beauvoir reasons that she is of an “age to die.” The hospital stay is longer than they expected, and the nurses help maman to eat, wash, and go to the bathroom. Beauvoir watches a swarm of people attending to her mother. Maman, who used to dress with consciousness, is made to wear nighties and is undressed several times a day as every nurse goes about her duty. Beauvoir is “jarred” by her mother’s nakedness, by how small and vulnerable she is.
